title: The Best Retirement Accounts for Self-Employed Americans
description: Solo 401(k) vs. SEP IRA vs. SIMPLE IRA.
content:
Being your own boss means you don't have an HR department to set up your retirement. It also means you don't have contribution limits holding you back. Self-employed Americans have access to the most powerful retirement accounts in the US tax code, allowing for contributions far exceeding the standard employee limit. Whether you are a freelancer, a consultant, or a small business owner, choosing the right structure can allow you to shelter up to $69,000+ per year from taxes. This guide compares the three main vehicles.

Key Takeaways

  • Solo 401(k): Generally the best option. Allows you to contribute as both Employee ($23k) and Employer (20% of profit). Has a Roth option. Requires no employees (except spouse).
  • SEP IRA: Easiest to set up. Employer contributions only (up to 25% of comp). No Roth option usually. Good for high income earners who want simplicity.
  • SIMPLE IRA: Good if you have a few employees. Lower contribution limits ($16k). Mandatory employer matching.
  • The 'Mega' Factor: Solo 401(k)s allow for the 'Mega Backdoor Roth' strategy (if the plan provider supports it), enabling massive tax-free accumulation.

Why It Matters (US Context)

You must open a Solo 401(k) by December 31st to contribute for that tax year, though you can fund it until Tax Day. SEP IRAs can be opened and funded up until the tax filing deadline (including extensions), offering more flexibility for procrastinators.

Head-to-Head Comparison

Which one fits your business model?

1. Solo 401(k) (The Winner)

  • Max Contribution: $69,000 (2025).
  • Pros: Highest possible contribution at lower income levels (due to Employee + Employer capability). Loans allowed. Roth allowed.
  • Cons: Paperwork. Must file Form 5500 if assets > $250k.
  • Best For: Solopreneurs engaging in aggressive saving.

2. SEP IRA (The Runner Up)

  • Max Contribution: $69,000 (25% of compensation).
  • Pros: extremely simple setup. No annual tax filing.
  • Cons: No 'Catch-Up' contribution. No Roth. No Loans. Must contribute equal % to eligible employees (expensive if you hire).
  • Best For: High income freelancers who want zero admin work.

3. SIMPLE IRA

  • Max Contribution: $16,000.
  • Best For: Small businesses with employees where a 401(k) is too expensive to administer.

Optimization Tactics

  1. The 'Side Hustle' 401k: Even if you have a day job with a 401(k), you can open a Solo 401(k) for your side hustle. You can't double-dip the 'Employee' limit, but you CAN contribute the 'Employer' portion (~20% of side profit) into the Solo.
  2. Spouse Employment: Hire your spouse. They can open their own Solo 401(k) under the same business. Now you can save $69k x 2 = $138,000 tax-deferred.
  3. Custodians: E-Trade, Schwab, and Fidelity offer free Solo 401(k)s. Vanguard's is more restrictive (no loans). Choose carefully.
  4. Deadline Awareness: If you miss the Dec 31 deadline for Solo 401(k), open a SEP IRA for the prior year to get the tax break, then convert to Solo 401(k) for the next year.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I have a Solo 401(k) with employees?

No. Only business owner + spouse. If you hire a full-time eligible employee, you must shut down the Solo plan and open a traditional 401(k), which costs money to run.

Does the deduction lower Self-Employment Tax?

No. It lowers Income Tax. You still owe the 15.3% FICA tax on your net earnings regardless of 401(k) contributions. (S-Corp structure solves this, not the 401k).

Can I do a Backdoor Roth with a SEP?

Be careful. A SEP IRA counts as a 'Traditional IRA' for the Pro-Rata rule. Having a large SEP balance blocks you from doing the Backdoor Roth tax-free. Solo 401(k) does NOT block it.
